source_document.body:
Do you know the difference between closed-weight models, open-weight models, open-data, and open-source? More importantly, do you think it matters? In a recent webinar, the CEO of CIQ , Gregory Kurtzer, was joined by Addison Snell, CEO of Intersect360 Research, to discuss an emerging issue in the AI market: Unknown risk of model failure due to closed-data training. (e.g., not knowing where the model talking to your customers learned its manners, if at all.) The lack of open-data provenance in popular Foundation models may introduce risk for many organizations that are integrating AI into their business processes.
The OpenWALDO project from CIQ is designed to bring “open-data” to the AI training arena as a way to increase trust and reduce risk in the AI market and community. As the webinar transcript describes the project is designed to bring open-data, open-source software, community, and public governance to the mysterious practice of training AI models. Further background can be found in the HPCwire article entitled What is OpenWALDO and Why Did Greg Kurtzer Need to Create It?
The transcript is based on the full video . The following is a shortened transcript that highlights some of the important insights discussed by both Greg and Addison.
Kevin: Welcome, everybody. And thanks for joining us today. We’re going to be talking about OpenWaldo. And you know what it means to have greater visibility and control over the AI models that your organization uses. And, of course, today joining us is Gregory Kurtzer, founder and CEO of CIQ and founder of OpenWALDO. And we also have Addison Snell, CEO of Intersect360 Research. My name is Kevin Jackson, and I am an analyst here at Intersect360. Greg and Addison, it’s great to have you here.
Kevin Jackson is an analyst with Intersect360 Research and formerly the editor of AIwire
Greg: It’s good to be here. Thank you, Kevin.
Addison: I always have great conversations with Greg, so this is fun for me. Let’s see how it goes today.
Greg: Absolutely. Great meeting. Interesting or weird.
Addison: You know, we’ll see where we go.
Kevin: Exactly. Well, you know, we’re going to explore what OpenWaldo does. You know why it matters for enterprises and what it could mean for how organizations evaluate and adopt AI going forward. So, you know, just to get us started, I’m going to put this question to both of you. But Greg, I’d like to hear your response first. If I’m running a model on my own infrastructure, I’m keeping my data private. Yeah, I might feel that I’ve handled it or I’ve checked the sovereignty box, but actually what am I still not controlling? And why does that matter?
Greg Kurtzer is the creator of OpenWALD O
Greg: There are a lot of aspects about running your own model, trusting your own model, trusting the infrastructure that that model is running on. And how do you check that box on sovereignty? And it’s even more than sovereignty. It’s ownership, it’s control, and it’s visibility, knowing what it is doing. So a lot of organizations are pulling open-weight models and then running them locally. We don’t know what a lot of these open-weight models have been trained on. We don’t know what they’re going to do in a variety of different situations. We don’t know what the code they’re going to be writing is, or what the interfaces and tooling they’re going to be using are. We don’t know what they’re going to, what it’s going to be doing with it. I mean, that’s kind of, it’s kind of one of the, I’ll say, benefits of a non-deterministic system such as an LLM. But at the same time, even though it’s non-deterministic, they definitely have kind of directions that they will pull toward based on the statistics of what they were trained on. So you need to know kind of what’s inside your model. You need to have proper boundaries, guardrails, and sandboxing of your tooling, your agents, etc., and you need to know what everything is doing. So you need to have proper infrastructure visibility and monitoring.
Addison Snell, CEO of Intersect360 Research
Addison: Yes. I mean, that’s the way we’ve seen it in our research: of course, people are organizations. Enterprises are already moving to adopt AI, as, you know, they want to adopt it. They want the productivity gains. They want the efficiencies. But what I like about what you said, Greg, about control, a lot of that really comes down to risk. And we’ve seen this with any new technology that gets adopted, whether it’s, you know, high-performance computing, modeling and simulation, or whether it’s cloud computing or whether it’s the Internet, right? What are the risks that are involved? And it’s not that I have to have no risk. I just want to know what the boundaries are on the risks. Am I protected on the downside, on cost? Am I protected on the downside on what catastrophe might happen, right? It’s basically the way you put it. And the topic that’s in the popular press right now is all around regulation, the regulatory environment. What we find in our surveys is that people feel like they’re kind of okay with understanding what the different regulatory environments are, but they need to know that they’re stable, right? And, you know, how do I control my intellectual property? How do I control any of my downsides? And that’s what having my own model kind of feels like. It gives me more of a sense of control. I think, you know, regardless of where you stand on the regulatory debate right now, we need more regulation. We need less regulation. I think what a lot of organizations want is predictability. And I think what a lot of organizations want right now is, you know, well, I think the result is: can regulation even stay ahead of AI right now? If I’m going to sit back and wait for regulation to explain everything to me, I’m going to get too far behind. That’s just part of the risk environment right now. So how do I go forward with a model, feel like I have some kind of semblance of control, and manage my risk while I chase the productivity gains?
Greg: You bring up such a good point. A few of them, but one of them that I want to touch on is the data. So for an AI model, whether you’re running it on-prem or you’re running a frontier model, you need to give it data in order to get a good response, right? So inside of your prompt or inside of your tooling, it has to have information about what you want to be asking it. And if you’re asking it things about your core business, core products, trade secrets, things under NDA, like you have to include bits and pieces of that- if not the entire IT in its entirety in your prompt in the context, which means you very well might be leaking data. And this gets really bad when we start talking about agents and, even more than agents, all of the tools that the agents write that are scattered all over the infrastructure or even on the Internet that have access to your data. And then what’s securing those tools, what’s securing those applications, and then what’s securing the agents to make sure that they are being maintained within their guardrails and that we’re not doing something, you know, like hacking another site or hacking a foreign government.
Addison: Well, right. I mean, there are so many analogies with that, that I expect my AI to act within certain boundaries, just like anything else that I hire or employ. If I tell my personal assistant to go pick up my dry cleaning and my personal assistant gets there and finds the dry cleaner to be unexpectedly closed, I don’t expect my personal assistant to smash the windows and break in order to follow the directive to go pick up my dry cleaning, right? Without at least checking with me first. “Hey! It’s closed. Dude, how bad do you need it? Do you want me to write?” That would be outside the normal realm of what I expect. Now, that’s where we talk about guardrails and how the models behave. And I guess you can train a model to do whatever you want. Maybe you’re someone who wants it to go break in, but that should be auditable in some way. Right? Did you give it that directive or not? And you know, when we design a car, we expect it to behave in certain ways. Which doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally cause damage with a car, but you want it to be built so that you don’t accidentally cause damage with a car. I think that’s the point.
Greg: That brings up a whole other can of worms, by the way, which is accountability and liability. And where does that exist? Kevin, I’m going to defer to you on that particular can of worms to keep us on track.
Kevin: I t’s a conversation we’re all having right now. I think something that Addison says all the time, and I’ll fill in here, is that if you use a new technology to commit fraud, it’s not that we need to write a new law. Fraud is already illegal, right? It’s something that Addison brings up quite often — we already have laws in place that perhaps we could be using and strengthening, but it’s a whole debate that could suck up this whole hour if we wanted to.
Addison: Well, I think that’s not the point. Right. But when it comes to control and auditability, there’s been a lot of discussion of things like open weights. But then what’s the difference between open weight and open-source, and what do you get out of it?
Kevin: That’s where I was driving toward. I’m seeing a lot of people use open weight and open-source interchangeably, and they shouldn’t. Greg, can you tell me what the difference is? And why does that difference matter to a company, or a business?
Greg: Well, the first thing that I want to mention is it’s actually really confusing. And it’s confusing because, if you think, I mean, several different aspects, if you think of open-source software, the open-source premise was kind of written around the notion of open-source software. So we kind of have a really good, firm understanding of what that means when we’re applying it to software. You basically think about it as you have the source of something, whether that’s source code or, you know, it’s been debated if data is considered the source in programs, but you have your source, and then you have your output. And if your source is open-source, the output is open-source. Kind of, that’s the definition of open-source, right? With weights, AI weights, it’s different, and it’s different because we have a bunch of open-source tooling that we’re using to build kind of the foundation and architecture of our models. And then we take the input data, the source, which is not open, and use the open-source tools to create binary weights. And these binary weights then are distributed in some cases under an open-source license. So that means you can do whatever you want with the binary weights, but you don’t know what went into those binary weights. The source for it is not available. So I’m a purist when it comes to open-source, in the most fundamental way.
Greg: And as a result of it, I think of it as any source that you’re using to create an artifact needs to be open for that artifact to be called open-source. And so for an AI, that means that your training data- that’s the corpus of data you’re using. It is the composing and the build tools that you’re using to create your model. And if you just have the open weights, well, open weights are great. Please don’t get me wrong on this. I love the fact that we have open weights. A lot of the complaints that we have around open weights, a lot of the concerns, the transparency, Addison, that you were mentioning. Well, the binary weights are kind of like a black box. You can’t ever go from those binary weights. And then understand how they are produced. And so, as a result, we need to kind of be thinking about this from the perspective of what’s inside those, and if we want to mitigate the concerns of what it means to be an open model. Well, we’ve got to go back to the source, and we’ve got to have trust in everything that was used to create this model. And if we have that, then we can fundamentally call ourselves an open-source model, but without that, open-weight models are not bad, but they’re definitely not open-source.
Addison: Yeah. I think what you’re getting at, Greg, is it hits right at that question that we had about mitigating risk because the large organizations or even small organizations we talk to generally have processes in place for when something goes wrong. They want to trace back to how it happened, whether it’s a product defect or a failure in policy somehow. And, you know, there was some customer harm. You want to know not just how to close this gap, but what caused that to happen. What allowed that to happen? And with AI and some of these open-weight models, you don’t know how they were trained. There’s that worry that I’m going to trace it back and I’m going to get back 1 or 2 steps, and the answer is going to be, well, the AI did it, and it stops there. Well, why did the AI do that? And I’d kind of like to know why the AI did what it did, so that I know that I’m not going to repeat the same mistake, which isn’t necessarily really fear-driven. It’s just kind of best practice in any organization to be able to audit why we’re doing the things that we’re doing, particularly in areas that are considered to be strategically important. When we polled organizations, enterprises, medium and up to large enterprises on where they’ve adopted AI, we found it really prevalent in areas like coding and office productivity and, you know, that kind of thing. But it’s least prevalent in areas having to do with product development and engineering and R&D, which is supposed to be the promise of AI, right? It’s going to help us predict the weather and find new products and cure diseases and all these areas that we’re used to associating with high-performance computing and scientific discovery. That’s where AI is least deployed right now. It’s where the biggest gap is. And I think this notion of control and auditability is one of those pieces that’s been missing.
Addison: I mean, look, I’m not a doomer about this. I think there will be things that happen that are bad. Just like with any new technology, if you invent a car, you’re going to have car crashes. Overall, the car accelerates a lot of things and does a lot of good for humanity. Right? And you could say that about any new technology. Overall, I think organizations do want to chase the productivity gains here. People are adopting it. The question I keep coming back to is then: how do I mitigate the risk? How do I control or understand the downside? And in order to activate the upside, because AI should be accelerating discovery in all of these ways, it just feels like there’s been a piece missing to help get to that level of control. That gives me confidence to move it into those areas of forward-leaning R&D and scientific discovery.
Kevin: Absolutely. And, let’s talk about that missing piece. Let’s make it a little bit more concrete with this discussion about OpenWALDO. What can an organization do with OpenWaldo today? And what decision would it help that organization make? How is this going to further that organization’s mission?
Addison: So start by saying what OpenWaldo is. We just dropped this term in here.
Kevin: Please, Greg, why don’t you give us a good, deep discussion of the entirety of this?
Greg: Yeah, absolutely. So kind of going back to the open-source versus the open weights discussion, there isn’t really a way for community members to kind of join together and band together to start creating an AI from scratch. This would involve, as I mentioned before, the AI corpus or training material. This involves data that you’re going to be potentially post-training on and teaching it, for example, how to interact with an API, how to interact with a data structure, how to actually respond properly. So all of these things have to go into the training data, into the corpus. And then you have your tooling, and then all the tooling kind of brings this whole thing together. And then you, of course, need a community around this to be able to say, well, you know, I’m going to bring in this piece of data, or I’m going to work on this tooling, or I’m going to be reviewing this corpus, or I’m going to be looking at the different types of compose files that we have for creating different types of AI models. And I want to ensure, and again, I use this metaphor, tongue-in-cheek humorously, but just to make sure there are no Terminator movie scripts in it or books and whatnot on the AI being not aligned with human humanity and laws, right? So let’s make sure that we are putting laws into this. Let’s make sure that we are putting appropriate ethics into this and having that transparency and visibility. Addison, what you’re mentioning is super important because if I have the ability to choose between two types of models, and I know what went into both of them, I can make an educated decision on which model I want to run, and I can make that decision as a company now, managing some of my risks and compliance.
Addison: I think that’s exactly the point that we were building up to. You’ve created an AI bill of materials that I can investigate, and that the community, as it will, if you think about the open-source community and this becomes an AI community that’s contributing to this corpus, if you’ve got a question about it, take a look. Here it is under the covers. And boy, when I think back to how open-source software really took off, you know, going back to the advent of Linux in the mid to late 1990s, what happened was you had this terrific open-source community of programmers that were then all working on something together. And it didn’t take very long before that raced to the forefront; this is what we’re going to build our organization on.
Greg: The entire free software and open-source movement is that we all have the ability to look at the source for whatever artifacts we’re talking about, right? Whether that source is software. And again, I’m a purist. So whether that source is software and code or whether that’s whatever went into the artifact itself, if you have that ability to see into it, you now have a level of trust that doesn’t require faith. It requires it because you could see it.
Kevin: Absolutely. And this kind of brings me to something I wanted to discuss here. Most companies, most enterprises, most businesses, they’re not training foundation models themselves, right? And if I’m using or maybe fine-tuning someone else’s model, how can OpenWaldo help me? And what would it take to use it in order to benefit my organization?
Greg: T raining a model, I want to say, is a very difficult thing to do. There are a lot of things that can go wrong, and it is exceedingly expensive to have the appropriate hardware to train a model. And an interesting aspect about it is, and I’m just going to kind of talk about this very superficially, but training a model and running your model are two different things, right? So you have your training side, which is where you’re taking all that input data, and you’re kind of managing the orchestration of how you’re building that model, and you’re running it on a very large, very expensive resource, usually with many, many GPUs. On the light side, this is probably tens of millions of dollars to build one of these systems. The large frontier AI labs have ridiculously large investments in their training infrastructure. And I want to be very clear: you could be using that training, that infrastructure, and after months of training, you realize that the model went askew, or your training plan went askew, and you’re either starting over or starting over from the last known good checkpoint. And it’s an expensive, very frustrating, very high-risk kind of process to train a model. And a lot of times you end up with a model that comes out the other side.
Addison: Yes, and the question was around how does OpenWaldo help? And I think you laid the groundwork for that, Greg, because, you know, I don’t really want to train a whole foundation model myself. Let’s take something simple, like a chatbot. I want to use that for my business, whether it’s internal or for my customers. I don’t need to retrain basic human vocabulary from scratch. I do have to give it some knowledge about my products and my business, including my own internal jargon that’s important to me, that might not be in the general corpus, right? So there is some training, but I’d like to start from an auditable, understood foundation because I don’t want to find, you know, later that my chatbot has been, you know, picking up a habit of sexually harassing the people who interact with the chatbot because it learned from the Internet. Right. That would be bad. I don’t want that to happen. I don’t want to train that part. I’d like to have something that comes in starting out good, and then I’m going to specialize it.
Kevin: It’s a great discussion. It’s something that I’m sure we’ll touch back on. But, you know, just to keep this rolling, we’ve kind of been circling around this, but I’d like to dive into it specifically. Say I’m a decision-maker at my company, and I’m deciding on how I want to move forward with the project. How should I decide whether to buy a supported AI product or build on open-source? What should drive that choice?
Greg: So, I’ll jump in on that one. I would make the relation back to what we’ve been doing in open-source for decades now. There are companies that stand behind products that will give you guarantees, assurances, and take the liability on, in many cases, for those products to at least do what those products say that they’re going to do to a reasonable extent. And, when organizations are buying part of their software infrastructure, that’s part of what they’re buying; even if it is 100% based on open-source software, you’re buying that, that commercial relationship; in a more direct sense, you’re buying the throat to choke, and you are mitigating your risks and compliance needs by doing so. Now, if a company wishes to go direct to open-source and download an open-source operating system or build their own kernel or, you know, run without a support contract, without a commercial agreement. What they’re basically ending up with is, well, they’re taking on the liability themselves. Now, with open-source, it’s not an unreasonable thing in many cases to take on that liability yourself because you can see what’s in it; you know what that software is going to do. And you can audit if you’re so inclined and/or able; you can audit that code and make sure that it’s at least as good as, as you know it, it is supposed to be, with what we’re seeing right now with open weights.
Addison: I think, Kevin, just the fact that you’re asking the question underlines the point that there’s going to be segments for all of these things, just like there has been ever since Linux and the early debates in the late 1990s about whether to trust my enterprise on open-source software. I think we found over time that a lot of people did, or what I want is something that’s open-source, but I want a supported version of the open-source, right? But either way, taking the boom in AI now and all of the dialogue we’re already having around open weights and saying, what about something more like open-source with an open corpus and a community-driven effort? I mean, I think this is something that really is going to take off. OpenWaldo is kind of an early mover here; first to market has the opportunity. Is it going to be OpenWALDO in the future? I guess that’s for CIQ and to try to drive their product. But we haven’t seen this before. And I think for those who are worried about, you know, us or Western technology and what’s going on with the Chinese, I mean, you know, imagine if this were a Chinese product right now, would there be concern about what the control around it is and who’s auditing it? I think the idea that you have an open community, open corpus, open weight, open-source, like, here’s something I can understand and build AI on it. Companies will evaluate how much control, how much support they want over time. But an open community effort around AI, I think we’ve seen enough in the past to know that this is an idea that ought to take off.
Greg: You know, we’ve been we introduced OpenWALDO; we talked about it. And you just kind of gave this string of openness that I think is really important. And it’s funny because I gloss over this so often because, like, maybe I’m so close to it, but the name itself is actually really cute. Not because Waldo is cute. It’s because, well, maybe, but it’s because WALDO stands for open weights, open artifacts, open licenses, open data, and open origins. And when you put that all together, that’s basically what we’re ending up with in terms of what it means to be a truly open-source model. And when we’re talking about the corpus, we’re talking about the data and the origins of that model. So, anyway, just wanted to put that out there that all those things together is really where OpenWaldo got its name.
Kevin: W e’re just talking about transparency, and I’m interested in something: making the training data inspectable is one thing, but having the expertise to evaluate it is another. How does an enterprise turn that transparency into confidence? And who should do the checking?
Greg: I’ll take another stab at this. Not to dominate, I’ll go back to how open-source works today. We, holistically, as a community of enterprises and individuals and people, we all rely on open-source software every single day, whether you know it or not. And there are, I mean, I can’t even tell you how many millions and billions of lines of software that we are relying on that is open-source. We have several ways of trusting that because there are examples of malicious actors, bad actors trying to infiltrate open-source communities to try to get malicious code into the open-source ecosystem. And this has happened 100%. And we’ve learned lessons as a result of that. Are the lessons foolproof? No, they’re not. But we’re continuously learning. And if you look at the amount of contributions that we get, it’s an incredibly small amount of contributions that have actually turned out to be malicious, and what we’ve been able to do is leverage things like the developer certificate of origin (DCO), leveraging accountability, understanding who the contributors are, and being able to monitor those contributions with reviews, code reviews, data reviews, etc., before we allow anything into the corpus, whether it’s open-source software or the OpenWaldo corpus.
Greg: That creates trust: the fact that you can, even though many people might not be able to, either technically, or it may just be too much data. The Linux kernel has tens of millions of, I think, tens of millions of lines. It’s definitely in the millions. I don’t know if it’s tens of millions. I need to go back and check that now. But there’s so much code in there, and it requires such specific expertise that even many software developers who are very senior in their roles cannot audit the Linux kernel. They can’t audit the core toolchains of the C library and the compilers and whatnot within every single operating system that we’re using that’s based on 0open-source. Can’t do it, but specifically knowing that others can is where you start to develop confidence and trust. And when we’re talking about data, like what’s in OpenWaldo, we’re not talking about the goalposts being a little bit shifted because we’re not talking about software and code that people can, anybody can review; in this case, we’re actually just talking about such a mass quantity of data. It’s hard to review. We’re talking about hundreds of billions and trillions of tokens going into an AI corpus.
Addison: Yeah, I think you really highlighted important things there, Greg, with regard to how these things get adopted. And I would start by looking at what processes we already have in place, again, not reinventing things, but then we’ll find that processes have to evolve somehow. My, I like that you were talking about software development in general. Vibe coding is one of these areas that’s really taken off. And there’s this idea of, look how much faster I can produce software. Well, but any professional software engineer will tell you that writing the code is one part of it. You know, have I checked it for dependencies against all the other modules? Is it well documented? How about security checking all that software? Right. Who’s doing all that as you pile it on? Is it another AI that’s doing the security check? What’s that process like there? A lot goes into software engineering beyond just, ” Hey, I produced all this code that needs to be checked. It needs to be, you know, integrated in certain ways. And there should be a process for that. Maybe the process needs to evolve because you’re producing software so much faster. And I can extend that to scientific discovery and, you know, hey, I’m producing papers so much faster now because AI is helping with the research. Okay. What about peer review? Right? I’ve just put out 2000 papers. Who’s doing the peer review on 2000 papers? Is peer review important? It’s been a cornerstone of our scientific process.
Addison: I want that data. Right. And it was like this change in policy of how they want to do their testing, which implied some extra cost, but it was a worthwhile cost in order to get the gain. Now AI is going to be a little different, but it’s kind of the same. What I want is to start with my existing processes and figure out how to adapt the policies to get the AI gain, but still keep confidence and, in fact, build confidence that the AI is taking me in the right direction. And again, having an auditable or open AI that I can look at and say, this is how we got to where we are. That’s what we already went through with modeling and simulation. Right? How do we build the confidence that the simulation is good? It rhymes with the idea that how do I build confidence that the AI is good means evolving my process. So I feel confident in the peer review. I feel confident in the product test. I feel confident in the customer interaction. You know, if I have a customer service rep, I train them, and I monitor them to make sure that they’re interacting with the customer the right way. Chatbot, same thing, right? I want to train them. I want to monitor them. But the process has to evolve to incorporate the AI if I’m going to really take advantage of it.
Kevin: We’re, we’re running out of time here.
Greg: I have a plug before you close.
Kevin: Please go right ahead.
Greg: So Addison and I are going to be sitting down together again at Supercomputing ( SC26 ) this year. If you’re not familiar with Supercomputing, you need to check it out. Supercomputing is one of the coolest conferences in existence. And Addison and I are gonna be sitting down and doing a panel. We’re going to be having discussions like this. We’re going to be taking more information, more questions from the crowd. And we really are a lot of fun on stage together. I’m just saying. So you all should come and join. If you’re headed to Supercomputing, definitely join us. If you’re not going to Supercomputing, you’re missing out. You should.
Addison: Greg’s going to prompt me to tell a joke while we’re up there. I’m pretty sure I told him. I told him I have a couple of dad jokes at the ready. Absolutely.
